content: For effective monitoring and evaluation of operations and interventions, including health-related interventions, it is essential to adapt existing health data collection systems used by UN agencies and NGOs. These systems must be pre-configured to incorporate core national indicators and standards, such as those for tuberculosis (TB), and to facilitate national reporting. Monitoring TB prevention and care should address both immediate humanitarian needs and contribute to national TB surveillance and monitoring systems. In humanitarian emergencies, the Global Compact on Refugees emphasizes the importance of collecting national data disaggregated by nationality or refugee status. Transitioning from paper-based systems to digital formats can be challenging in some countries. However, as nations adopt case-based electronic reporting systems for TB, this transition becomes more feasible. Standardized TB forms, registers, and reports used by National TB Programs (NTPs) in moderate and high-burden settings, including primary healthcare staff, are critical for effective data management. In some regions, significant progress has been made in implementing electronic case-based reporting systems, but many countries have yet to make this transition. For example, in Kenya, the Dadaab refugee complex, established in 1994 during the Somali civil war, has become a model for integrating TB services into national systems. Supported by UNHCR, the International Rescue Committee (IRC), the Kenya Red Cross (KRC), and Médecins Sans Frontières (MSF-Switzerland), TB services in Dadaab comply with national policies and guidelines. Case-based TB data is submitted electronically to the NTP database via the TIBU application, an Android-based platform launched in 2012. TIBU has been updated to include laboratory data, drug resistance information, and contact tracing, and is used nationwide, including in remote areas like refugee camps. To improve TB care and prevention, it is crucial to use collected data locally for real-time improvements and emergency responses. This includes adapting TB services based on population characteristics and conditions in emergency settings. Mechanisms for safely sharing TB patient data across borders are essential, especially during humanitarian emergencies when refugees may move between countries. TB patient cards should be provided to ensure continuity of care, and referral information should be transmitted to national authorities when patients are relocated. Supervision of TB services is critical to ensure quality care, particularly during emergencies. Supervisors should be trained in key monitoring elements, and standardized TB checklists can facilitate effective supervision. Engaging communities, civil society organizations, and community health providers is vital in emergency settings. Community leaders and organizations can help identify individuals with TB symptoms, support treatment adherence, raise awareness, and advocate for better access to TB diagnostics and care. The WHO has developed operational guidance, case studies, and tools for community-based TB care under the Engage-TB initiative. For example, in Burkina Faso, the Ministry of Health and the Global Fund have supported the training of community health workers to detect TB early, trace contacts, and provide treatment support in camps and communities hosting internally displaced persons (IDPs). This approach has reduced the number of people lost to follow-up and improved treatment success rates. In emergency settings, private and non-NTP public healthcare providers may already be delivering TB care. These providers, including public hospitals, correctional facilities, and private institutions, can be integrated into public-private mix (PPM) models to serve affected populations. However, a well-functioning PPM framework with supervisory structures is necessary to ensure effective engagement. A TB component should be included in national emergency communication plans. This involves preparing concise TB messaging toolkits in advance, tailored to specific audiences such as media, affected populations, and host communities. These toolkits should address TB risks, stigma, co-infection with HIV, and the importance of diagnosis and treatment adherence. Communication materials should be available in the languages of affected populations to ensure clarity and understanding. Effective airborne infection control measures are critical to prevent TB transmission during emergencies. National infection prevention and control policies should include specific TB measures, supported by clear plans, adequate facilities, and surveillance of TB among healthcare workers. Research and innovation, such as rapid diagnostics and AI-assisted radiography, should prioritize vulnerable populations and be integrated into emergency preparedness and response efforts. Collaboration with academic partners and operational research can help address barriers to care and improve adapted models of TB care in emergency settings.
